title: Nepal PM Balen Shah Thanks India for Flood Aid as Death Toll Passes 1,100
excerpt: In his first parliamentary address on the crisis, Nepal's prime minister detailed the government's response and praised India's assistance including DNA testing support as nearly 4,000 people remain missing.
body:
• Nepal PM Balen Shah addressed parliament on September 2, detailing the government's flood response and thanking India for timely aid including DNA testing and a medical rescue team.
  • The death toll has risen to 1,127 with nearly 4,000 people still missing, including 590 foreign nationals from 39 countries.
  • Over 11,993 people have been rescued so far, with joint Nepal-India-China teams working at devastated hydropower stations where hundreds remain trapped.
  • More than $42 million in international aid has been pledged, with India dispatching 57.6 tonnes of relief material since the August 26 glacier collapse.

Nepal Prime Minister Balen Shah addressed parliament on Wednesday for the first time since the devastating Bhotekoshi floods struck on August 26, thanking India for its swift humanitarian assistance as the death toll climbed past 1,100 and rescue operations entered their second week.

"We are with the country in these difficult times," Shah told lawmakers, presenting a detailed timeline of the government's response. He described how emergency teams were alerted within minutes of the disaster, with Army helicopters deployed and rescue squads mobilized by mid-morning on the day the glacier collapsed.

India's Role in the Response

Shah singled out India's contributions to the relief effort. New Delhi dispatched an 11-member medical rescue team and 57.6 tonnes of relief material in the days following the disaster. India has also been assisting Nepal with managing the bodies of those killed, including providing DNA testing capabilities and helping establish a laboratory for victim identification — a critical need given the scale of the destruction.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi spoke with Shah shortly after the floods, offering condolences and pledging "all possible humanitarian assistance." Nepal Health Minister Nisha Mehta confirmed India's DNA testing support on Wednesday, calling it essential for identifying victims in areas where floodwaters obliterated entire settlements.

"In this hour of crisis, we have accepted the reality that the country's leadership must provide courage, support and reassurance, not tears. We have no alternative but to fight with determination and courage, and we are fighting."

— Balen Shah, Prime Minister of Nepal

Scale of the Disaster

The confirmed death toll has reached 1,127, according to Nepal Police, with 3,916 people still listed as missing. Among the missing are 590 foreign nationals from 39 countries, including over 100 Indians and 37 NRIs who were in the region when the glacier collapsed.

The flood originated from a glacier collapse on the Tibet border that sent a massive wall of ice, rock, and mud surging through the Bhote Koshi river valley, destroying settlements and critically damaging at least a dozen hydropower projects across the Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading districts.

Over 11,993 people have been rescued so far. Shah told parliament that 279 workers had been freed from hydropower project sites, where joint rescue teams from Nepal, India, and China are using heavy machinery, excavators, and temporary bridges to reach those still trapped. An estimated 639 people remain stuck inside several devastated hydropower stations.

International Response and Climate Warning

International aid worth more than $42 million has poured into Nepal since the disaster, with contributions expected to increase. South Korea is sending a 44-member emergency relief team to support search operations in Rasuwa, where nine of its nationals working at a hydropower project are among the missing. China has also dispatched DNA testing experts and additional relief supplies including drones and water purification equipment.

Shah used his parliamentary address to draw attention to the climate dimension of the crisis. "The time has come for us to strongly raise before the international community the disasters we are experiencing as a consequence of climate change," he said. China's state broadcaster confirmed that the flood was "caused by glacier instability under the long-term effects of global warming."

Diaspora Impact

The disaster has directly affected India's diaspora connections with Nepal. Over 100 Indian nationals and 37 NRIs were among the nearly 400 tourists reported missing in the initial days. India and Nepal share deep geographical, cultural, and people-to-people ties, with open borders that facilitate significant cross-border movement. The Indian government's rapid response — coordinating rescue operations and providing specialized support — reflects the strategic importance of the bilateral relationship during humanitarian emergencies.
